description: I am a solo developer from Indonesia, passionate about technology, Earth science, and interactive experiences. My project, TELLUVOX, transforms NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into dynamic, synchronized sound through immersive 3D visualization and real-time sonification. I am interested in web development, data visualization, audio programming, and scientific storytelling. This is a solo project, so I am not currently looking for team members.
summary: TELLUVOX is an Earth Jukebox: a web application that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into synchronized, real-time music. Users pick a visualization, press play, and every frame is analyzed as it appears. Its colours, brightness, shapes, spatial density and change drive a musical ruleset, so colours become chords, shapes become voices and motion becomes rhythm. Where NASA publishes a numeric colour bar, TELLUVOX reads the colours back into estimated values, so warmer oceans literally sound higher. Every sound is paired with plain-language text, read-aloud descriptions, explore-by-touch tones and optional vibration, so blind and low-vision users can explore Earth science by ear, by touch and in words. It addresses the challenge by making EIC visuals multi-sensory and accessible, while staying honest about what the sound does and does not measure.
details:
What it does TELLUVOX plays NASA Earth Information Center visualizations like records in a jukebox. Nine of the visualizations listed in the challenge resources are built in, from sea surface currents and night lights to lightning, aerosols, CO2 and forest height. Users can also drop in any EIC video or image sequence. As the frames play, TELLUVOX analyzes each one and generates music in real time, always synchronized with the image on screen.

How it works

  1. Frame capture: each displayed frame is drawn to an offscreen canvas and downscaled for fast analysis. Videos are sampled into evenly spaced frames that keep their real timestamps.
  2. Visual analysis: brightness, average colour, a deterministic k-means colour palette, warm/cool hue balance, luminance entropy, contrast and edge density, bright-area coverage (Otsu threshold), connected shapes with their size, elongation and orientation, horizontal and vertical balance, and frame-to-frame change and motion.
  3. Musical ruleset: 14 mappings turn measurements into music. The dominant colour picks the chord, warm or cool colours pick major or minor, complexity adds sevenths and ninths, hue picks melody notes on a pentatonic scale, texture sets note density, bright coverage sets tempo, change adds rhythmic ticks, the number of shapes sets polyphony, elongation sets staccato or legato, upward motion makes the melody rise, horizontal balance pans the sound, and saturation shapes the timbre. One key and consonant harmony keep it musical rather than noisy.
  4. Reading NASA colour bars: for visualizations with a published numeric legend (sea surface temperature 0 to 32 °C, forest canopy height 0 to 50 m), TELLUVOX samples the official colour bar and estimates values from matching pixels. The median value raises or lowers the melody. Values are always labelled as estimates with the share of matched pixels. Legends that could not be read reliably are shown for reference only, with the reason stated.
  5. Synthesis and sync: the Web Audio API generates a bass drone, a chord pad, a melody instrument and percussive ticks, with reverb and a limiter. Each frame's phrase is scheduled on the audio clock so sound and image change together.
  6. Globe: a 3D Earth drawn from Natural Earth coastlines with the real day/night terminator for the current time. Global flat maps are draped onto it only after their alignment with the coastlines has been verified numerically.

Benefits

  • Accessibility: Earth visualizations become perceivable without sight. Every frame has a plain-language description that can be read aloud. Any area of an image can be explored by touch or keyboard, each area playing its own tone. Vibration follows the amount of change. All controls work with a keyboard and screen reader.
  • Discovery: sound reveals rhythm and change over time, such as a sudden shift between frames or a warm current drifting across the globe.
  • Honesty: synthetic demo data is clearly labelled, NASA resources are credited individually, and colour is only interpreted as a physical value when NASA's own colour bar supports it.
  • Documentation: the full per-frame analysis can be exported as CSV or JSON, and soundscapes can be recorded as audio files.

What we hope to achieve We want anyone, including blind and low-vision people, students and museum visitors, to be able to listen to our changing planet. Next steps are using the per-frame dates that NASA publishes, turning categorical legends such as aerosol types into separate instrument tracks, and loading any EIC visualization directly by its page number.

Tools and technologies TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, the Web Audio API, the Canvas API, d3-geo and topojson-client with Natural Earth data, the Web Speech and Vibration APIs, MediaRecorder, Vitest (99 automated tests), ffmpeg for extracting frames from the NASA videos, and Netlify for hosting.

Source code : https://github.com/rasidi3112/telluvox
